# **Image Similarity and Near-Duplicate Detection for Local-First 2D Digital Artwork Catalogs**

For a local-first catalog of 2D digital artwork spanning 10,000 to 1,000,000 files, no single similarity representation maintains high precision and recall across JPEG recompression, resizing, cropping, text overlays, and sketch-to-finished progressions1. Classical perceptual hashes (pHash, dHash, wHash, and 256-bit PDQ) screen exact resizes and lossy recompressions at low compute and tens of megabytes of RAM, yet fail catastrophically on crops—dropping PDQ to 0% Recall@1 on a 70%-side centered crop—and suffer sharp precision collapse as recall increases1. Pretrained vision embeddings such as DINOv2 and SigLIP recover geometric resilience, with DINOv2-Small retaining 91% Recall@1 on the same 70%-side crop and patch-pyramid decompositions (Patchify) reaching 65.16 mAP on the ILIAS instance-retrieval leaderboard3, but they introduce semantic collisions across distinct drawings of the same character or scene while increasing index RAM roughly 10× for INT8 quantized vectors to \~40–60× for FP32/FP16 descriptors2.  
Practical local-first deployment therefore relies on a multi-stage filtering funnel backed by stateful human review rather than a single distance cutoff7. Open-source systems approach this pipeline from complementary priorities: Czkawka (and its active Slint frontend Krokiet) maximizes multi-threaded Rust scanning throughput using image\_hasher, 4 KB prehash caching, and ascending Hamming-step BK-tree grouping paired with a visual diff comparison tool8, whereas Hydrus Network wraps a 64-bit DCT pHash VP-Tree inside a persistent four-state relational graph (potential, duplicate, alternate, and transitive false positive) designed for illustration variants7.  
A critical evidentiary gap constrains these choices: no peer-reviewed benchmark identified in the reviewed literature evaluates classical perceptual hashes, sub-region hashing, DINOv2, and SigLIP side by side on a dedicated 2D digital illustration deduplication corpus such as Danbooru. Quantitative precision-recall comparisons below therefore synthesize peer-reviewed copy-detection and instance-retrieval benchmarks on photographs and object catalogs—including DISC21, ILIAS, PHASER, USENIX Security 2026 hash cryptanalysis, and MDPI evaluation studies1—together with an October 2026 open-license benchmark preprint (arXiv:2610.04151, 98,985 registry images across 79 edits)2 and specialized anime line-art correspondence and sketch-based image retrieval (SBIR) studies19.

## **Domain Peculiarities of 2D Digital Illustration and Artwork**

Deduplicating 2D digital art breaks core statistical assumptions built into photographic perceptual hashes and natural-image vision encoders. Most classical perceptual hashes—including standard 64-bit pHash as well as Czkawka’s Mean, Gradient, DoubleGradient, and Blockhash algorithms—strip color information and operate purely on grayscale luminance1. In an illustration archive, grayscale hashing causes color-shifted variations and palette swaps to look identical to the original file22, collapsing intentional recolorings—which curators typically want preserved as related alternates rather than deleted—into near-zero Hamming distances7.  
Large uniform canvases, flat cel shading, and borders introduce a second structural failure mode. Comics, character sheets, and web reposts frequently contain wide white backgrounds, black letterboxes, or site frames. In compact binary hashes, large uniform regions force low-frequency DCT coefficients or mean-intensity bits to correlate across completely unrelated artworks, driving up false positives at permissive thresholds (Max Difference ≥ 10 in Czkawka or Hamming distance ≥ 10 in Hydrus)7. An arXiv perceptual-hash distribution study (2212.08035) confirms this shift quantitatively: adding borders pulls 64-bit pHash pairwise normalized Hamming distances downward from a baseline mean of 0.4904 (median 0.5000) to 0.4283 (median 0.4375), while visible watermarks shift the mean to 0.4704 (median 0.4688), narrowing the separation between true duplicates and unrelated images23. Even dense self-supervised vision transformers exhibit uniform-background pathologies: vanilla DINOv2 generates high-norm artifact tokens in low-informative background regions, degrading spatial matching unless retrained or augmented with test-time "register" tokens24.  
Fine ink linework and subtle facial or costume details also expose resolution limits in pretrained vision models. Standard ViT backbones downsample inputs to 224×224 pixels25, smoothing away thin hatching and small expression edits. On the CVPR 2025 ILIAS 100M instance-retrieval benchmark (as summarized by atlas.scime.ai), input resolution outweighed parameter scaling for SigLIP: a smaller SigLIP ViT-B evaluated at 512 px or 724 px outperformed a larger SigLIP ViT-L evaluated at 256 px or 384 px17. Finally, artwork catalogs operate under a multi-tier ontology rather than binary duplicate deletion: collectors routinely retain works-in-progress (WIPs), recolors, hairstyle swaps, and costume variations alongside canonical renders, requiring deduplicators to group related works without erasing artistic history7.

## **Quantitative Performance Across Transformations and Benchmarks**

### **Classical Perceptual Hashes: Multi-Scale pHash, dHash, wHash, and PDQ**

Classical perceptual hashes trade geometric invariance for speed and minimal storage. Standard 64-bit pHash downscales a grayscale image to 32×32, computes a type-II 2D Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), extracts the top-left 8×8 low-frequency coefficients, and thresholds each against the block median to produce a 64-bit digest compared by XOR Hamming distance1. Multi-scale or higher-bit extensions—such as Meta’s 256-bit DCT-based PDQ23 or Czkawka’s size-32 and size-64 configurations22—expand bit capacity to reduce random collisions and encode finer spatial frequency structure22. By contrast, dHash (and Czkawka’s Gradient/DoubleGradient) encodes relative brightness differences between adjacent downscaled pixels, conferring robustness against uniform global illumination shifts1, while wHash applies a Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)23.  
Peer-reviewed evaluations expose sharp recall boundaries across these algorithms. In an MDPI comparative benchmark (mdpi.com/2079-9292) on the UKBench Near-Duplicate subset, AHash, dHash, pHash, and wHash all suffered an abrupt drop in precision as soon as recall moved beyond very low operating points1. Across two evaluation runs in the DFRWS 2024 PHASER framework over the McKeown and Buchanan (2023) benchmark, 256-bit PDQ consistently ranked above 64-bit pHash, which in turn substantially outperformed wHash across both Hamming and Cosine distance metrics (unlabeled primary validation scores of 0.918 and 0.969 for PDQ, 0.905 and 0.931–0.932 for pHash, and 0.817 and 0.820 for wHash, with accompanying error columns moving inversely)15. Platform documentation from Alibaba Cloud Dataphin notes wHash is comparatively robust against repeated compression, noise, and slight blur29, while a small-sample 2023 *International Journal of Network Security* test on mural photography found dHash \> pHash \> aHash across clipping, blur, sharpening, rotation, and resizing (with dHash yielding 48.44% false similarity on distinct-but-similar pairs vs. 70.31% for unimproved pHash)30.  
Despite acceptable stability under JPEG recompression and proportional resizing15, global frequency and wavelet hashes break under cropping1. In Kazempourradi et al.’s October 2026 arXiv preprint (2610.04151) evaluating 98,985 registry images, a centered crop retaining 70% of each side (49% area) dropped **PDQ to 0% Recall@1**2. Microsoft’s 1152-bit PhotoDNA suffers the same weakness against cropping despite high compression resilience31, and a USENIX Security 2026 study demonstrated that PhotoDNA near-collisions appear after ![][image1] to ![][image2] evaluations depending on threshold, undermining earlier unsubstantiated estimates of a 1-in-50-billion false-positive rate14.

### **Crop-Aware Sub-Region Hashing vs. Patch-Pyramid Embeddings**

Partitioning images into sub-region tiles restores recall on cropped excerpts, but naive classical tile hashing triggers severe false-positive amplification. Under a multiple-comparison regime with ![][image3] tiles per image, cross-comparing tiles between every pair of images expands pair-level collision risk by roughly ![][image4]4. Even under an idealized unbiased-bit binomial model (![][image5]), expanding a single 64-bit pHash (![][image6]) to a 14-tile spatial pyramid (![][image7], mirroring 1×1 \+ 2×2 \+ 3×3 grids) across 1,000,000 catalog files increases expected random false-positive image pairs from 2.26 to 442 at Hamming distance ≤ 6, and from 139 to 27,300 at distance ≤ 8; at ![][image8] tiles, expected false positives reach 125,000 at distance ≤ 84. In real illustration catalogs where flat white or shaded background tiles share identical low-frequency structure, empirical collision rates exceed this uncorrelated floor unless tile descriptors use ≥256 bits, filter low-entropy tiles, or verify spatial geometry.  
Dense patch-pyramid retrieval (Patchify, WACV 2026\) solves cropped matching without brittle region proposals or expensive keypoint matching5. Patchify partitions gallery images into structured multi-scale grids—L0 (1×1 \= 1 patch), L1 (+2×2 \= 5 patches), L2 (+3×3 \= 14 patches), or L3 (+4×4 \= 30 patches)—encodes each patch with a frozen vision transformer (DINOv2, SigLIP, or CLIP), compresses descriptors using Product Quantization (PQ or IVF-PQ), and ranks gallery matches by the maximum cosine/inner-product similarity between a single global query embedding and any gallery patch5. According to the HyperAI ILIAS benchmark leaderboard, Patchify with DINOv2 achieves **65.16 mAP**6, while natively exposing which specific grid cell matched (LocScore) for human verification5. Similarly, on the large-scale ILIAS 100M benchmark, adding OWLv2 crop reranking over a DINOv3-L first stage raised mAP@1000 from 26.5 to 42.0 (+15.5 percentage points) and Recall@1 from 55.0% to 76.0% (+21.0 pp), though extreme 3.3× scale/camera-distance shifts still degraded even the strongest backbone (SigLIP-2-L) to 0.12634. On DISC21, a February 2026 *International Journal of Computer Vision* study ("Tracing Copied Pixels and Regularizing Patch Affinity in Copy Detection") similarly reports that local patch-affinity matching raises µAP from 72.6% (global descriptor) to 88.7% (matcher)35.

### **Pretrained Vision Embeddings and Copy-Specific Descriptors**

Dense foundation embeddings invert the trade-off of perceptual hashing, preserving strong geometric recall while shifting the primary risk toward semantic over-matching2. In Kazempourradi et al.’s October 2026 arXiv benchmark across 79 transformations at a strict, registry-size-independent pair-level false-match rate (FMR) of 10⁻⁷, copy-detection models trained on non-commercial data detected up to **75.5%** of transformed images, while **DINOv2**—the highest-performing permissively licensed (Apache-2.0) backbone—detected **65.0%**2. On the 70%-side centered crop that drove PDQ to 0% Recall@1 and dropped the binary ISC21-derived ISCC Image-Code to 12% Recall@1, **DINOv2-Small retained 91% Recall@1**2. Specialized self-supervised copy descriptors like SSCD outperform classification-oriented self-supervised features by a wide margin2, and relational self-supervised distillation with hard-negative loss (RDCD, 2024\) recovers \+5.0%, \+4.9%, and \+5.9% µAP over baseline distillation on DISC21 across compact 64-, 128-, and 256-dimensional vectors where naive PCA degrades accuracy37.  
DINOv2 and SigLIP exhibit distinct architectural biases relevant to text overlays and artistic progressions:

* **DINOv2 (Self-Supervised Visual Backbone):** Pretrained purely on curated images without text supervision39, DINOv2 concentrates instance-level spatial discrimination in late-layer attention heads (such as Layer 10, Head 2, which separates pixel-identical copies by spatial location more selectively than SigLIP)41. Combined with test-time or trained registers24 and attention optimization (MaO, NeurIPS 2025, which improves zero-shot retrieval to 70.20% mAP vs. 65.22% for CLIP with 0.03 s/object offline refinement)42, DINOv2 excels at structural correspondence. In the anime domain, a 2025 arXiv line-art colorization system feeds 518×518 line drawings into a frozen DINOv2 encoder (1024-d feature maps) fused with a U-Net and superpixel pooling to propagate colors accurately across reference and target frames19. On zero-shot domain generalization, however, DINOv2 lags behind weakly supervised text-aligned models on ImageNet-R and ImageNet-Sketch39.  
* **SigLIP and SigLIP-2 (Sigmoid Image-Text Contrastive Backbones):** By replacing CLIP’s cross-batch softmax normalization with pairwise sigmoid loss, SigLIP scales cleanly to larger architectures (such as SigLIP-SO400M) and supports multilingual alignment in SigLIP-243. On ILIAS 100M, zero-shot SigLIP ViT-L achieved 19.6 mAP@1k for image-to-image retrieval (confirmed independently by an ECCV 2026 benchmark paper44), while an atlas.scime.ai summary of the CVPR 2025 paper reports SigLIP2 ViT-L reaching 20.8 zero-shot (rising to 31.3 with UnED linear adaptation, and SigLIP ViT-L rising from 19.6 to 28.9 with adaptation and 35.6 with AMES local reranking)17. In sketch-based image retrieval (SBIR), zero-shot global vision embeddings still struggle with the gap between monochrome line drawings and shaded color renders, requiring triplet-loss adaptation (S3BIR-CLIP and S3BIR-DINOv2 perform comparably once fine-tuned21), textual-inversion prompt composition45, or sketch-guided spatial masking46. Because SigLIP aligns high-level concepts across styles, it surfaces semantic alternates and stylized variants more readily than pixel-identity hashes, but risks falsely conflating distinct illustrations of the same character or composition2.

## **Precision-Recall Trade-Offs and False-Positive Scaling at Local Catalog Scale**

Benchmarking deduplicators solely with per-query ranking metrics (mAP@k or Recall@1) masks operational failure in local collections. All-pairs comparison across ![][image10] files checks ![][image11] pairs—roughly 50 million pairs at ![][image12], 5 billion at ![][image13], and 500 billion at ![][image14]—meaning tiny per-pair false-positive rates rapidly overwhelm manual review. The NeurIPS 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (DISC21) formalized this global calibration requirement via **micro-Average Precision (µAP)** over all pooled query-reference predictions16:  
![][image15]  
Unlike macro-AP, µAP requires similarity scores to remain directly comparable across all queries16. Kazempourradi et al.’s 2026 soft-bindings benchmark reinforces this lesson by setting operating thresholds on held-out negatives for registry-independent pair-level FMRs down to 10⁻⁷: even at 98,985 registry images, near-copies in product catalogs dominated false matches, and classical geometric verification offered **no net improvement** once false-binding rates were held equal under matched calibration2. Furthermore, embedding an invisible watermark pushed the learned binary ISCC Image-Code past its match threshold on **62.0%** of tested images, illustrating how sensitive compact binary descriptors can be to subtle pixel-level perturbations18.

Because adjacent low-frequency image descriptors are correlated rather than uniform random bits, empirical false positives in illustration archives appear well below theoretical thresholds. Hydrus Network’s operational documentation explicitly reflects this inflection: Hamming distances 0–4 isolate resizes and costume variants cleanly, useful recall drops off past distance 8, and querying at distance 10–12 floods queues with unrelated portraits or geometric silhouettes7. Expanding to 256-bit digests (such as PDQ or Czkawka size-16 hashes) provides over 12 orders of magnitude of theoretical headroom at an equivalent 18.8% normalized Hamming threshold (3.21 × 10⁻²⁵ vs. 2.28 × 10⁻⁷), buying substantially cleaner separation even under correlated artwork margins4.

### **Local-First Memory, Disk, and Ingestion Budgets**

Quantized vision indexes fit comfortably inside consumer desktop RAM up to 1,000,000 files, whereas unquantized FP32 multi-patch pipelines become memory- and compute-bound4. No unified peer-reviewed ingestion benchmark comparing Rust perceptual hashing against quantized DINOv2/SigLIP ONNX runtimes was found; however, a Hugging Face model card evaluating a fine-tuned **DINOv2-Small (384-d, \~86.6 MB)** ONNX export in a CPU notebook environment reports **\~45 ms/image** (\~22.2 images/s single-stream) with only 0.00002 maximum probability divergence from PyTorch48, while a RoboLabs deployment blog estimates Intel OpenVINO delivers 20–25% CPU speedups over generic ONNX Runtime53. By contrast, real-time evaluation of heavyweight SigLIP models shows latency exceeding 150 ms per frame on constrained hardware54, generally favoring GPU FP16 batching for SigLIP-SO400M43.

## **Architectural Teardowns of Open-Source Deduplication Pipelines**

### **Czkawka and Krokiet**

Czkawka (qarmin/czkawka, with Krokiet serving as its actively developed Slint GUI as legacy GTK development closes after v12.012) is engineered as a fast, stateless Rust batch cleaner11. Its similar\_images engine delegates hashing to the image\_hasher crate (v3.1.1 in recent builds), unconditionally enabling fast\_image\_resize for SIMD downscaling and hamming-bitwise-fast for hardware popcount comparisons10. Format support covers standard rasters alongside photography and illustration formats including embedded JPEG previews in RAW files, HEIF, JXL (via register\_image\_decoding\_hooks()), AVIF, QOI, and RAW decoding through rawler9.  
**Multi-stage candidate filtering** proceeds across four deterministic stages:

> 1. **Filesystem & Size Pruning:** Directory traversal filters hardlinks (hide\_hard\_links), applies path exclusions including the \$TRASH preset (\#1962), strips excluded extensions (\#1184), and ignores files below a minimum byte floor (16 KB default in Krokiet GUI; 8 KB in CLI duplicate mode)—a safeguard that can silently omit small icon assets or lightweight monochrome sketches9.  
> 2. **Prehash & Disk Cache Lookup:** Before full pixel decoding, Krokiet enables a prehash step (--use-prehash-cache in CLI) that hashes up to the first and last 4 KB of large files to skip unchanged assets, loading previously computed hashes from cache\_similar\_image\_\*.bin10. Scans remain interruptible because partial hash progress flushes to cache60.  
> 3. **Luminance Perceptual Hashing & Geometric Invariance:** Images are decoded, resized with selectable FilterType (e.g., Lanczos3), and converted to hashes via HashAlg (Mean default, Gradient, VertGradient, DoubleGradient, Median, or Blockhash) at bit dimensions 8, 16 (Krokiet default), 32, or 6422. Recent releases added GeometricInvariance to catch rotated or flipped variants (updating cache compatibility)9.  
> 4. **Distance-Stepped BK-Tree Grouping:** Hashes are inserted into a Burkhard-Keller tree (bk\_tree)8. As documented in Czkawka 3.3.0 release notes on Reddit (with similarity grouping logic later refined in \#1685), because BK-trees cannot delete keys mid-search efficiently, Czkawka sweeps ascending integer Hamming steps from 0 up to max\_distance (Max Difference 0–40, defaulting to 10 in Krokiet and 5 in CLI)8. Files matched at strict distances are marked and excluded from looser passes, curbing runaway transitive chaining8. Optional "reference folders" restrict comparisons asymmetrically so trusted archive files are matched only against incoming directories22.

**Human-review explanations and artwork gaps:** Krokiet adds a dedicated image comparison tool to inspect visual differences (\#1888), custom selection popups (\#1809), sortable size/dimension/similarity metadata, and separate move-to-trash versus permanent deletion controls (\#1900)9. However, Czkawka lacks a **persistent inter-scan relationship database**: dismissing a false positive (such as grayscale-collapsed artwork or shared white margins22) does not suppress that pair in subsequent scans, nor can it record "alternate" WIP relations. Massive digital canvases (e.g., 23,420×30,560 px JPEGs reported in issue \#1500) also present resource and stability edge cases during decoding62, and all built-in hashes remain blind to color edits and cropping22.

### **Hydrus Network**

Hydrus Network (hydrusnetwork/hydrus) is a local-first booru media catalog built specifically around large personal illustration, comic, and animation archives7. Refactored to isolate visual hashing inside ClientImagePerceptualHashes (v620)65, its deduplication architecture pairs a single perceptual fingerprint with **stateful graph memory and high-throughput manual triage**.  
**Multi-stage candidate filtering** separates exact raster equivalence from approximate visual matching:

> 1. **Pixel-Duplicate Identification:** Hydrus tracks **pixel duplicates**—files with identical dimensions and byte-for-byte identical decoded pixel arrays despite stripped EXIF headers or metadata re-encoding—separating lossless container duplicates from perceptual approximations7.  
> 2. **64-bit DCT pHash & VP-Tree Search:** For non-identical files, Hydrus extracts a 64-bit DCT pHash representing "similar shape" and indexes digests in a **Vantage-Point Tree (VP-Tree)** for Hamming-radius queries7, with explicit handling for uniform blank comic pages (v686)66.  
> 3. **Distance Ladder & Dual Predicate Cross-Filtering:** Hydrus records the discovery Hamming distance (maximum search distance of pair) and advises clearing distance 0 first (resizes and JPEG recompressions), stepping to 4 (hairstyle or costume edits), and stopping at or below 8 (warning that 10–12 swamps queues with false collisions)7. Prospective pairs can be gated by dual tag/system search predicates—matching *at least one file*, *both files*, or *two distinct searches* (such as pairing system:filetype is jpeg with system:filetype is png to hunt down compressed scrapes of lossless originals)7.

**Human-review explanations and transitive relationship graph:** Hydrus’s defining strength is its **four-state persistent relationship model** and triage ergonomics7:

* **Duplicate Equivalence Groups with "King" Selection:** Marking (A duplicate B) merges files into a transitive cluster that tracks one highest-quality "King" file7. Default mouse bindings compress decision overhead (Left-click: keep better and delete other; Right-click: mark related alternates; Middle-click: undo)7. Rather than relying on brittle automated blur scores alone, Hydrus guides reviewers with domain-specific illustration heuristics: prefer older/original posts, higher resolution, **PNG over JPEG for screenshots and pixel/vector/line art (but JPEG over PNG otherwise)**, wider uncropped framing, absence of watermarks or site borders, and higher tag richness7.  
* **Alternate Holding Groups & Transitive False-Positive Propagation:** Related non-identical files (WIPs, recolors, costume swaps) are placed into **Alternate** groups7. False-positive decisions are stored between *alternate groups* rather than isolated files, propagating transitively: if (α alt β) and (ψ alt ω), marking (α fp ψ) automatically implies (α fp ω), (β fp ψ), and (β fp ω) are all false positives7. Across multi-variant illustration sets, this prevents combinatorial false-positive recurrence across future scans.  
* **Batch Scheduling:** Users switch between randomized checkpointed batches (\~100 pairs in mixed pairs mode) and connected-component queues (group mode, resolving every pair in a cluster before moving on)7. Hydrus’s primary technical constraint is its single global 64-bit pHash: it cannot surface heavily cropped panel extractions, rotated compositions, or rough line-art sketches whose low-frequency luminance differs sharply from final painted versions, and it lacks built-in pixel-diff overlays or dense patch-match highlights.

### **Tool Architecture Comparison**

| Architectural Dimension | Czkawka / Krokiet (Rust / Slint) | Hydrus Network (Python / Local DB) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Primary Fingerprints** | image\_hasher (Mean, Gradient, VertGradient, DoubleGradient, Median, Blockhash); hash sizes 8–64; GeometricInvariance9 | Exact decoded **pixel duplicates** \+ 64-bit DCT pHash7 |
| **Metric Search Structure** | **BK-Tree** swept across ascending Hamming steps 0..max\_distance8 | **VP-Tree** indexing 64-bit pHashes with stored pair search distance7 |
| **Pre-Filtering & Caching** | 4 KB head/tail prehash \+ binary disk cache; min file size (16 KB GUI); reference folders22 | Persistent database; dual tag/filetype predicate pair filtering (e.g., JPEG vs. PNG)7 |
| **Relationship State Model** | Stateless per-scan clusters; dismissed false positives reappear on future scans | Persistent 4-state graph: potential, duplicate (King), alternate, transitive false positive7 |
| **Human-Review Explanation** | Visual comparison tool (\#1888), side-by-side size/resolution tables, similarity levels9 | Checkpointed mixed pairs vs. group mode, 1-click hotkeys, art/format quality heuristics7 |
| **Core Artwork Blind Spots** | Grayscale-collapsed false positives, blank-margin matches, no alternate/FP memory, large-canvas decode pressure22 | Blind to heavy crops, geometric rotations, and divergent sketch-to-finished luminance |

## **Reference Multi-Stage Pipeline for Local-First Artwork Management**

Combining peer-reviewed precision/recall findings with Czkawka’s high-speed filtering and Hydrus’s relational graph yields a four-stage architecture suited to 10k–1M+ local 2D artwork catalogs:

> 1. **Stage 0 — Byte & Exact Pixel-Raster Deduplication:** Compute cryptographic file digests alongside decoded pixel-dimension hashes (Hydrus pixel-duplicate style7) after filtering zero-byte or corrupt files. This clears metadata-stripped reposts and lossless container repacks automatically with zero perceptual false positives.  
> 2. **Stage 1 — Multi-Core 256-bit Global Hash Screening (PDQ / DoubleGradient):** Compute 256-bit hashes (such as PDQ or Czkawka DoubleGradient at size 16\) backed by 4 KB prehash caching and an ascending-distance metric tree (VP-tree or BK-tree)7. Auto-crop uniform letterbox borders and isolate solid-color canvases before hashing to curb margin collisions22. At \~61 MB RAM per million files4, this fast pass resolves exact resizes and lossy JPEG recompressions cleanly15.  
> 3. **Stage 2 — Quantized Dense Vision & Patch-Pyramid Indexing:** For unmerged files, compute **DINOv2-Small with registers** (384-d INT8 HNSW \= \~488 MB for 1M files; \~45 ms/img measured in CPU ONNX benchmarks4). Where catalogs contain frequent cropped comic panels, bust extractions, or heavy watermarked frames, build a **Patchify-L2 (1×1 \+ 2×2 \+ 3×3) PQ16×8** index (\~641 MB at 1M) rather than naive sub-region perceptual hashes4. If sketch-to-finished discovery or text-guided alternate grouping is also required, maintain an auxiliary **SigLIP-B (at ≥512 px input resolution) or SigLIP-2** index strictly for *non-destructive alternate discovery* rather than automated deletion, preventing cross-character semantic collisions2.  
> 4. **Stage 3 — Explainable Human Triage & Transitive Graph Persistence:** Feed Stage-1 and Stage-2 candidates into Hydrus’s four-state transitive graph (Duplicate with format-aware King rules—favoring lossless PNG for crisp line/vector art—plus Alternate holding groups and transitive False Positive propagation across alternate sets)7, augmented with visual diff comparison (\#1888)9 for global matches and Patchify bounding highlights (LocScore)5 for cropped/overlay pairs. Surfacing *where* a match occurred and persisting every human decision eliminates repetitive review work across evolving artwork libraries.
